promise: See the mechanism that makes a surprising mathematical result inevitable.
audience: Curious teens and adults; begin with concrete objects and state necessary prerequisites.
personality: Playful mathematical workshop: curious, tactile, precise; viewer is an investigator.

identity.materials: Warm paper, solid ceramic-like pieces, restrained depth, crisp boundaries. Geometry used as proof stays exact.
identity.motion: Stable identities. Move, pair, cut, unfold and rearrange to expose relationships. Attention cues are distinct from mathematical state changes.
identity.voice: Warm curiosity; concrete statements; pause at consequential inferences. No constant hype.
identity.sound: Soft wood clicks and glass-like resonances; optional short resolving motif. Silence protects difficult reasoning; score changes with the episode.

hard_constraints: Preserve counts, areas, incidence and probabilities used in the argument.
Never encode mathematical meaning by color alone.
Keep essential objects and labels readable with captions and platform UI.
Identify simulations, examples and proofs accurately.
preferences: Let objects carry the opening question; avoid a branded intro delay.
Make the active mechanism large; use text to name an insight already made visible.
Keep the same material language but invent composition for each topic.
Treat the payoff as a visible resolution, then offer a small transfer case.
Prototype the hardest inference before complete production.
Carry object identity across explanation beats; a persistent heading is optional.
Review every member of a batch before its first publication.
Explain the mapping between views before using it as evidence.
Fade replacement phrases; do not morph unrelated letter shapes.
Declare and sample every critical transition through its end.
Use topic-specific settings within the shared material and color language.
Open with a consequential action and a prediction the viewer can actually make.
Give the hardest inference the largest useful workspace; retain a small orientation cue when zooming.
Author caption phrases as sense units; preserve exact spoken content and timing.
Use sparse action-linked sounds as a testable design choice, not an assumed learning benefit.

formats.visual-proof: A concrete puzzle resolves through an invariant or transformation.
formats.investigation: Predict, manipulate, discover the mechanism, test a new case.
formats.simulation: Show the process and uncertainty; distinguish numerical evidence from proof.

examples.prefer: Move identified objects into explicit one-to-one pairs; keep unmatched objects visible.
examples.avoid: Display the final formula over unrelated motion.

examples.prefer: Move the same exact pieces without scaling them.
examples.avoid: Morph unequal regions until they look equal.
examples.reason: Aesthetic deformation must not counterfeit conservation.

examples.prefer: Reduce sound and hold the relevant relationship while the viewer reasons.
examples.avoid: Add a whoosh or cut merely because a fixed interval elapsed.
examples.reason: Pacing follows cognitive work, not a universal timer.

examples.prefer: Keep the marked wheel visible through orbit, center trace and radius comparison. See examples/mechanisms/references/coin.
examples.avoid: Reset to a text slide after revealing two spins.
examples.reason: The viewer can track the same object while its explanation changes.

examples.prefer: Move the original 62 squares into 30 adjacent dark/light pairs and two visibly unpaired squares. See examples/mechanisms/references/domino.
examples.avoid: Replace pairing with two independent counted grids.
examples.reason: A one-to-one correspondence should be visible, not asserted.

examples.prefer: One active workspace; object-attached short labels; resize the workspace between exploration and proof. Short boundary tones, dry proof narration. See docs/research/MECHANISM-DIRECTION.md.
examples.avoid: The same title/diagram/formula stack in every scene or decorative clicks unrelated to action.
examples.reason: Channel identity comes from consistent decisions, not identical layouts.

examples.situation: A concrete example becomes an abstract representation
examples.prefer: Keep one shared control or identified quantity visible; demonstrate its effect in both views.
examples.avoid: Replace the object with a completed graph and assume the viewer can translate.
examples.reason: Understanding the correspondence is part of the learning task.

evidence.status: Design hypothesis informed by adjacent evidence; no audience validation yet.
evidence.validation: Test recognition, appeal, comprehension and production effort separately across topics.
